--- title: "[Tweedie]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Tweedie family with log link. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L13-L344){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python Tweedie(p=1.5) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The Tweedie family is an exponential dispersion model whose variance function is a power of the mean, `V(mu) = mu^p`. It is most widely used for `1 < p < 2`, the compound Poisson-Gamma case: a distribution with a point mass at zero and a continuous, right-skewed density on the positive reals. This shape is a natural fit for aggregate insurance claims (many policyholders have zero claims, and the rest have positive, Gamma-like claim amounts), precipitation totals, and biomass or catch data with structural zeros. Whittaker also supports `p > 2` for purely positive, heavy-tailed continuous data (including the inverse Gaussian case at `p = 3`; see `InverseGaussian`). The Poisson (`p = 1`) and Gamma (`p = 2`) boundary cases are excluded here — use `Poisson` or `Gamma` directly for exact likelihood computations at those values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.5]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Variance power. Must satisfy `1 < p < 2` (compound Poisson-Gamma, the typical choice for insurance-type data with zeros) or `p > 2` (positive continuous, heavy-tailed data). Values of exactly `1` or `2` are rejected because they correspond to `Poisson` and `Gamma`, which have simpler, exact deviance and likelihood formulas. If `p` is unknown, use `tw()` to estimate it from the data instead of fixing it here. ::: ## Notes {.doc-notes} The link is the natural logarithm: $$ g(\mu) = \log(\mu) $$ The variance function is a power of the mean: $$ V(\mu) = \mu^{p}, $$ which interpolates between `Poisson`-like behavior (`p` near 1) and `Gamma`-like behavior (`p` near 2), or heavier-tailed behavior for `p > 2`. The unit deviance is $$ d(y, \hat\mu) = 2 \left[ \frac{y^{2-p}}{(1-p)(2-p)} - \frac{y\,\hat\mu^{1-p}}{1-p} + \frac{\hat\mu^{2-p}}{2-p} \right], $$ summed over observations to give the total deviance. Because the Tweedie density has no closed form for `1 < p < 2`, the log-likelihood is evaluated using the Dunn & Smyth (2005) saddlepoint approximation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Fit a GAM to compound Poisson-Gamma data with a point mass at zero: ::: {#d8f6c375 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import whittaker as wk rng = np.random.default_rng(0) n = 300 x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n) mu = np.exp(1.0 + 0.5 * np.sin(x)) p = 1.5 scale = 1.0 lam = mu ** (2 - p) / (scale * (2 - p)) alpha = (2 - p) / (p - 1) gamma_scale = scale * (p - 1) * mu ** (p - 1) n_claims = rng.poisson(lam) y = np.array( [rng.gamma(alpha, gamma_scale[i], size=n_claims[i]).sum() for i in range(n)] ) data = {"x": x, "y": y} model = wk.GAM("y ~ s(x)", family=wk.Tweedie(p=1.5)) model.fit(data, method="REML") print(model.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` GAM fit summary ============================================================ Formula: y ~ s(x) Family: Tweedie(p=1.5, link='log') Observations: 300 Coefficients: 10 Parametric coefficients: Term Estimate Std.Err t value p-value ------------------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- (Intercept) 1.0177 0.0492 20.686 < 1e-16 Approximate significance of smooth terms: Term EDF Ref.df Chi.sq p-value ------------------------ ------ ------ ---------- ---------- s(x) 4.44 5 69.085 1.589e-13 Total EDF: 5.44 Deviance: 349.6177 Null dev: 436.9088 Dev. expl: 20.0% GCV score: 1.208856 Scale est: 1.186925 AIC: 1236.44 BIC: 1256.59 ``` ::: ::: ## Attributes {.doc-attributes}
Name Description
p Variance power $p$ in $V(\mu) = \mu^p$.
scale_known Whether the dispersion parameter is fixed. Always `False` for Tweedie.
### [p]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Variance power $p$ in $V(\mu) = \mu^p$. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} Determines the shape of the Tweedie distribution: `1 < p < 2` gives the compound Poisson-Gamma case with a point mass at zero, `p = 3` corresponds to the Inverse Gaussian, and other `p > 2` give heavier-tailed positive continuous distributions. ::: ### [scale_known]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether the dispersion parameter is fixed. Always `False` for Tweedie. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [scale_known]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} The dispersion `phi` is estimated from the data during fitting rather than fixed, independently of whether the variance power `p` itself is fixed or estimated (see `TweedieEstimated`). ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
deviance() Total Tweedie deviance, the (weighted) sum of `unit_deviance`.
initialize() Starting values for `mu`: `y` nudged away from zero.
link() Apply the log link: $\eta = \log(\mu)$.
link_derivative() Derivative of the log link: $g'(\mu) = 1/\mu$.
link_inverse() Apply the inverse log link: $\mu = e^{\eta}$.
log_likelihood() Tweedie log-likelihood via the Dunn & Smyth (2005) saddlepoint approximation.
simulate() Simulate Tweedie-distributed response values with mean `mu` and dispersion `scale`.
unit_deviance() Per-observation Tweedie deviance contributions.
variance() Tweedie variance function: $V(\mu) = \mu^p$ for the current variance power `p`.

[mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional prior weights, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The total (weighted) deviance. ::: ### [initialize()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Starting values for `mu`: `y` nudged away from zero. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L323-L341){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python initialize(y) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Since the log link requires strictly positive `mu`, values (including structural zeros typical of compound Poisson-Gamma data) are pushed away from zero to avoid `log(0)` on the first P-IRLS iteration. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values (non-negative), shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Starting values for `mu`, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [link()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Apply the log link: $\eta = \log(\mu)$. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L109-L122){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python link(mu) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. Must be positive. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Linear predictor values $\eta = \log(\mu)$, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values (non-negative), shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. [scale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dispersion parameter $\phi$. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional prior weights, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The total (approximate) log-likelihood. ::: ### [simulate()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Simulate Tweedie-distributed response values with mean `mu` and dispersion `scale`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L280-L321){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python simulate(mu, scale, rng) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} For `1 < p < 2` (compound Poisson-Gamma), a Poisson number of claims is drawn for each observation and each claim's size is drawn from a Gamma distribution, matching the point mass at zero characteristic of this regime. For `p > 2`, values are drawn directly from a Gamma distribution matched to the Tweedie mean and variance. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Mean (fitted values), shape `(n,)`. [scale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dispersion parameter $\phi$. [rng]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [np.random.Generator]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A `numpy.random.Generator` instance. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Simulated response values, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [unit_deviance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Per-observation Tweedie deviance contributions. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L194-L221){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python unit_deviance(y, mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Computes $d_i = 2 \left[ \frac{y_i^{2-p}}{(1-p)(2-p)} - \frac{y_i\,\hat\mu_i^{1-p}}{1-p} + \frac{\hat\mu_i^{2-p}}{2-p} \right]$ for the current variance power `p`, with the convention that the first term vanishes when $y_i = 0$. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values (non-negative), shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Per-observation deviance contributions, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [variance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Tweedie variance function: $V(\mu) = \mu^p$ for the current variance power `p`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/docs-cookbook/whittaker/families/tweedie.py#L157-L170){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python variance(mu) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Variance values $\mu^p$, shape `(n,)`. :::
